description: We're Project Andromeda, a team of engineering students from Tecnológico de Monterrey.
summary:
Andromeda is an iOS app that lets anyone listen to NASA's view of our planet. It turns Earth Information Center visualizations into music, so people who are blind or have low vision can experience climate data that today reaches them only as the word "Image."

We sonified 50 NASA visualizations across five collections: Oceans, Ice, Air, Land and Stars. They include sea surface temperature, global CO2, tree height from GEDI, lightning seen from the Space Station and Hubble star clusters. Our sound engine follows the method NASA used for its Westerlund 2 sonification. A line sweeps each image from left to right, higher means a higher note, brighter means louder, and left and right in the image play in your ears. Every instrument is a real recording.

The app works like a music player built for listening with your eyes closed. Before each session it introduces every sound, and you can ask "What am I hearing?" at any moment. An AI DJ with a human voice learns from your likes and plays the next session for you. It is fully accessible with VoiceOver.

Climate change affects everyone, so its data should be for everyone.
details:
What it does

Andromeda is an iOS app that turns NASA visualizations of our planet into music, so people who are blind or have low vision can explore climate data by ear. It works like a music player. Sessions are grouped into collections (Oceans, Ice, Air, Land and Stars), and each session is a NASA visualization with its own sonification. Today the app has 50 sessions, from sea surface temperature and global CO2 to forest height measured by GEDI and lightning seen from the International Space Station.

How it works

Our sound engine follows the method NASA used to sonify Westerlund 2. A line sweeps the image from left to right, higher in the image means a higher note, brighter means louder, and the position in the image is the position in your ears. We tuned the engine against NASA's own Westerlund 2 audio until it reached 0.91 in audio similarity, where NASA's audio compared with itself scores 0.95. Every instrument is a real recording, and some sessions use real field recordings, like wind, songbirds and rainforest for tree height, or thunder and rain for lightning. On screen, the reading line bends where it meets light, so it traces the same light that becomes notes.

Before each session, the app introduces every sound and what it means. During playback, the listener can ask "What am I hearing?" or repeat the legend. When a session ends, an AI DJ with a human voice picks the next one based on what the listener liked and has heard, says why in one sentence, and plays it automatically. The DJ prepares its pick before the session ends, so there is no silence between them.

Benefits and intended impact

43 million people are blind and 295 million live with moderate to severe vision loss (The Lancet Global Health, 2020). For them, a screen reader turns a NASA image into a single word: "Image." Andromeda gives them the same data as everyone else, as an experience they can enjoy and understand. It supports UN SDG 10 (inclusion of people with disabilities), SDG 4 (equal access to education) and SDG 13 (climate awareness).

Tools we used

  • iOS app: Swift and SwiftUI, AVFoundation for audio and video, VoiceOver and haptics
  • Sonification engine: Python with NumPy and SciPy, real instrument samples and a measured concert hall reverb
  • Backend: Flask API with an Azure SQL database that stores the catalog of collections and sessions
  • AI DJ: Google Gemini picks the next session and writes the line, ElevenLabs gives the DJ its voice
  • Sign in with Google, or listen as a guest
  • Data: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, NASA GIBS and Hubble imagery (NASA and ESA)
  • Hardware: Mac for development and iPhone for testing

How it is creative

Instead of describing a chart, we made the planet something you listen to like an album. The DJ connects sessions the way a radio host connects songs, for example moving from carbon dioxide to the smoke of carbon monoxide from fires. Each dataset gets sounds that fit its meaning, so the forest sounds like a forest and a storm sounds like a storm.

What our team considered

  • Accessibility first: every screen works with VoiceOver, a two-finger double tap plays or pauses from anywhere, and we checked text and controls against WCAG AA contrast.
  • Scientific accuracy: descriptions come from NASA captions, and the AI can only use facts from our catalog, never invent numbers or places.
  • Sound that is music, not noise: notes stay in a musical scale, so the data is pleasant to listen to for a long time.
  • Privacy and security: API keys and database credentials live on the server, never inside the app.
  • Credits and licenses: every NASA visualization and every field recording is credited in the app.
